content:
OpenAI has today revealed how it is complying with the EU's AI Act, which requires providers of generative AI systems to mark AI-generated text in a identifiable manner. Here are the details.

A little background

A few months ago, Anthropic caused controversy when it announced that, in order to comply with the EU AI Act, Claude would watermark text by slightly tweaking word choice.

In simple terms, Claude would occasionally pick between synonymous words based on a hidden pattern, something Anthropic said had no practical impact on the meaning, quality, or readability of the answer.

Anthropic also built a detector that can spot the pattern in a piece of text and judge whether it was likely produced by Claude.

Since Claude's watermark is generated using a key specific to Anthropic's system, the detector cannot be used to judge whether text was produced by OpenAI or any other competitor.

At the height of the controversy, Anthropic stressed that Claude wouldn't be the only system adopting such measures, pointing out that several other major AI providers were implementing marking systems to comply with EU requirements.

Today, OpenAI has revealed its own approach, which while similar in methodology is far smaller in scope and scale.

OpenAI's text watermarking system

According to OpenAI, as of today, "API customers globally can opt in to enable text watermarking for specified models"; and the company "will be introducing invisible watermarking to eligible ChatGPT and Codex text outputs in the EU over the coming weeks".

Meaning for now, on the API side, text watermarking remains off by default; while on the ChatGPT and Codex side, it will initially only be available to eligible users in the EU.

OpenAI has also opened applications for access to its text watermark detector, initially limited to approved research organisations and expert bodies, and says it will continue to evaluate and refine the technology.

On accuracy, OpenAI is very clear that the detection still has significant limitations, with both false negatives and false positives possible, particularly with shorter text or content in certain domains, such as "areas like math where there's less flexibility in word choice".

Here's OpenAI's description of textGrain, its text watermarking technology:

The company also notes that, in addition to being harder to detect in shorter passages, the watermark degrades substantially with editing:

Interestingly, OpenAI found that when comparing watermarked and non-watermarked text, the watermarked output actually scored marginally higher on several benchmarks, although the company says there was no clear difference in overall performance.

Benchmark Unwatermarked text (Astra, max) Watermarked text (Astra, max) Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index 49.57 points 49.76 points AutomationBench 34.09% 34.86% DeepSWE v1.1 72.80% 71.68% Terminal-Bench 4.0 53.90% 56.06% Terminal-Bench Science 0.1 56.90% 60.00% BrowseComp 87.92% 87.35% HealthBench Professional 64.27% 64.60% GPQA Diamond 94.44% 93.94%

OpenAI also stresses that, beyond the drawbacks of false positives and false negatives (sic), watermarks "do not measure human contribution", "do not establish ownership or responsibility", "do not identify a user", and "do not verify accuracy".

OpenAI adds that "the absence of a detected watermark does not prove that text was human-written".

Finally, the company says it expects to revisit its approach as technology, standards, and evidence evolve, while continuing to research how watermarks hold up after editing and translation, and whether they can more specifically distinguish between "AI-assisted" and "AI-authored".
